title: The Eagle and the Arrow
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: An Eagle sat perched on a lofty rock, keeping a sharp look-out for prey. A huntsman, concealed in a cleft of the mountain and on the watch for game, spied him there and shot an Arrow at him. The shaft struck him full in the breast and pierced him through and through.

As he lay in the agonies of death, he turned his eyes upon the Arrow. "Ah! cruel fate!" he cried, "that I should perish thus: but oh! fate more cruel still, that the Arrow which kills me should be winged with an Eagle's feathers!"

questions.prompt: According to the passage, where is the Eagle perched at the start?
options: In the branches of a tree
On a cliff by the sea
On a lofty rock
On a fence post near a farm

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what is the Eagle doing while perched there?
options: Keeping a sharp look-out for prey
Resting after a long flight
Feeding a group of young eaglets
Watching for approaching storms

questions.prompt: According to the passage, where is the huntsman hiding?
options: Behind a fallen tree
Inside a small cave
Beneath a pile of leaves
In a cleft of the mountain

questions.prompt: According to the passage, where does the Arrow strike the Eagle?
options: In one of his wings
Full in the breast
Along his tail feathers
In his leg

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Eagle do as he lies dying?
options: He tries to fly one last time
He calls out to other eagles nearby
He turns his eyes upon the Arrow
He watches the huntsman walk away

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Eagle notice about the Arrow that kills him?
options: It is winged with an Eagle's feathers
It is unusually large for a hunting arrow
It is marked with the huntsman's name
It is broken in two after striking him

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the Eagle call his fate "more cruel still" upon seeing the feathers?
options: He realizes the huntsman stole the feathers from his own nest
He believes another eagle deliberately betrayed him
He is surprised that arrows can be made from feathers at all
He realizes that a feather from his own kind helped bring about his death

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why is the huntsman able to strike the Eagle successfully?
options: He challenges the Eagle openly before shooting
He remains hidden and watches patiently before taking his shot
He is guided to the spot by another animal
He waits until the Eagle is asleep to shoot

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "lofty" mean in "a lofty rock"?
options: Smooth and flat
Covered in moss
Very high up
Narrow and pointed

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable?
options: There is a bitter irony in being harmed by something drawn from your very own nature
Huntsmen are always more skilled than the animals they hunt
Eagles should never rest on exposed, high places
Feathers make arrows less deadly than other materials

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what is the huntsman on the watch for?
options: Firewood
Fresh water
A place to camp
Game

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how completely does the Arrow pass through the Eagle?
options: It only grazes his feathers
It pierces him through and through
It lodges just beneath his skin
It strikes his wing rather than his breast

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Eagle exclaim as he lies dying?
options: "Farewell, sky!"
"Beware, huntsman!"
"Ah! cruel fate!"
"My kingdom is lost!"

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why might the Eagle's death be considered especially bitter compared to an ordinary death by hunting?
options: The very feathers that once let him rule the sky now speed the weapon that kills him
He is killed by another eagle rather than by a human huntsman
He dies far from his nest, unable to return home
He is struck down before he can catch any prey that day

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the Eagle's final words suggest he now understands about the arrow's construction?
options: The huntsman had personally raised eagles to obtain feathers
The arrow was specially made just to kill him
Feathers make an arrow lighter but less accurate
Arrows were commonly fitted with feathers from birds like himself

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "perish" mean in "that I should perish thus"?
options: Escape
Die
Suffer briefly
Recover slowly

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: An Eagle escapes a huntsman's arrow at the last moment
A huntsman spares the Eagle after admiring its feathers
An Eagle is fatally shot and realizes, as he dies, that the arrow bears his own kind's feathers
An Eagle is wounded but survives to fly away
